result: {"decisions":[{"point":"D2","problem":"How to obtain evaluation labels for explanations of model behavior when true causes are unknown and open-ended explanations may be wrong.","did":"They derived every evaluation label from measured outcomes of resampled counterfactual prompt edits rather than from the investigator's explanations or judgement.","alternatives_named":["treating the open-ended explanations as ground truth","relying on the investigator's judgement"],"stated_reason":"Explanations are often partially incorrect, whereas counterfactual experiments give independently checkable outcomes, so labels stay valid regardless of investigator capability.","quote":"The explanations are often compelling, but many are likely to be partially incorrect or to miss important drivers of the behavior, so we do not treat them as ground truth or evaluation labels"},{"point":"D2","problem":"How to let interpretability tools be tested without the predictor trivially recovering the ground-truth counterfactual outcome.","did":"They restricted predictor agents to read-only access to the target model's internals, excluding steering and activation patching, and measured uplift over a transcript-only baseline.","alternatives_named":["allowing interventions such as steering","activation patching","editing the prompt"],"stated_reason":"The label is itself the outcome of an input intervention, so an intervening predictor could approximate the ground-truth experiment rather than predict its result.","quote":"We restrict predictors to read-only access to the target model’s internals. The ground-truth label is itself the outcome of an input intervention, so a predictor that is allowed to intervene, whether on inputs or on activations, could approximate the ground-truth experiment"},{"point":"D3","problem":"Whether the surprising null result of no uplift from interpretability tools is real or an artifact of predictor choice, hyperparameters or weak elicitation.","did":"They replicated with other predictor families, swept tool-call and token-position hyperparameters, tried prompt iteration and an overnight optimization loop, and tested on a reasoning-model target before accepting the null.","alternatives_named":["a different predictor family (GPT-5.5, Gemini-3.1-Pro)","hyperparameter sweeps","manual prompt iteration","an overnight goal loop"],"stated_reason":"To show the negative result is robust to predictor family, hyperparameters, and elicitation.","quote":"The negative result is robust to predictor family, hyperparameters, and elicitation. Replicating the evaluation with GPT-5.5 and Gemini-3.1-Pro as the predictor agent in place of Opus 4.8 gives the same qualitative results (Appendix C.3)"},{"point":"D5","problem":"How to interpret why the tools gave no uplift despite their outputs changing the predictor's answers.","did":"They analyzed NLA outputs with LLM judges and concluded that causal relationships between the edited feature and the behavior are almost never stated, while treating this analysis as only a qualitative diagnostic.","alternatives_named":["the predictor ignoring tool outputs","poor token selection by the agent","activations being inherently incomplete for causal claims","tools needing better elicitation or scaffolding"],"stated_reason":"Explicit 'X causes Y' statements appeared in only 0.6% of positive claims, and applying the judge to every transcript token left the rate near zero, ruling out poor token selection.","quote":"An explicit statement is almost never present, as it only appears in 0.6% of positive claims (3 claims out of 479), and 0.02% of selected NLA generations. This is also not due to poor token selection by the agent"},{"point":"D3","problem":"Whether quality filters applied to build the evaluation set drive the main conclusions.","did":"They applied three LLM-judge filters (concreteness, reproducibility, single-factor) for the main results but re-ran both main evaluations on the full unfiltered claim bank and released both versions.","alternatives_named":["using no filters","applying stricter filters"],"stated_reason":"To show the no-uplift and generalization results are not artifacts of the dataset filters.","quote":"The filters do not change our conclusions: evaluating every tested method on the full unfiltered claim bank leaves the no-uplift result intact (Appendix F). We release both the full unfiltered dataset and the filter code"},{"point":"D1","problem":"Whether the training gains on counterfactual prediction could merely reflect distillation from a stronger investigator model.","did":"They added a second target setting in which Qwen3.5-397B-A17B investigates itself, removing the capability gap between investigator and target.","alternatives_named":["only using Opus as the investigator for Qwen3-8B"],"stated_reason":"Improvement might reflect distillation from the stronger model, and a frontier model could realistically only be investigated by a model of roughly its own capability.","quote":"Because the training data comes from a much more capable investigator, any improvement may simply reflect distillation from the stronger model rather than anything specific to the training setup."},{"point":"D2","problem":"How to test whether a self-trained model has privileged access to its own behavior beyond what training data teaches.","did":"They ran the Binder et al. self-vs-cross-trained comparison with Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B, using identical, size-matched data for both predictors.","alternatives_named":["comparing only against the base model"],"stated_reason":"Both models learn from the same evidence, so a self-trained model outperforming the cross-trained one would indicate privileged access.","quote":"The standard test distinguishes these by comparing the self-trained model against a cross-trained model, a second model trained on identical data about the target (Binder et al., 2024)."},{"point":"D6","problem":"How strongly to claim privileged access is absent given conflicting prior results and a different, broader task distribution.","did":"They reported no evidence of privileged access but offered caveats, noting uncertainty about why results differ from Li et al. and that more data may be needed for such effects to emerge.","alternatives_named":["claiming privileged access is absent in general"],"stated_reason":"Privileged-access effects may be fragile, or a broader task distribution may require more training data before any privileged signal can be learned after the behavioral prior.","quote":"We are uncertain what explains the difference from Li et al. (2026), who find privileged access in the hint setting using our same model pair (Qwen3-8B and Llama 3.1 8B Instruct)"},{"point":"D4","problem":"Whether to treat open-ended explanation training as a success given weak and mixed results on two evaluation metrics.","did":"They reported the mixed results in the appendix, argued both metrics may understate learning, and treated an LLM-judge correctness measure as only preliminary because it is circular.","alternatives_named":["directly judging explanation correctness with an LLM judge"],"stated_reason":"The hint setting is a large distribution shift, simulatability depends on simulator capability, and the LLM-judge evaluation is circular since training and evaluation come from the same pipeline.","quote":"However, this evaluation is somewhat circular, as the training data and the evaluation are generated by the same LLM pipeline, so we treat it as preliminary evidence only."},{"point":"D1","problem":"Whether the evaluation proxy is worth building given that anyone with sampling access could simply run the counterfactual.","did":"They chose to build a proxy evaluation with clear ground truth whose questions mirror real use cases, accepting that performance is not directly useful.","alternatives_named":["evaluating hypothesis generation rather than hypothesis discrimination"],"stated_reason":"Interpretability tools are most needed where no ground truth exists, so a proxy with checkable answers is the only way to measure reliability; failing on it is a bad sign for harder cases.","quote":"Given that, we believe the useful thing to build is a proxy: an evaluation with clear ground truth whose questions have the same shape as the real use cases (given an unusual behavior from a model, explain why it happened)"}]}
